Proof search for formal mathematics
Entity-hallucination probes on the reviewer
Reward-hacking and shortcut monitors on experiment agents

Extracting physics from learned models to fix simulators (Goodfire discovery pattern)

Kilometre-scale weather and climate

R1:physical.title: Privacy auditing and membership inference
R1:physical.summary: Checking privacy or memorisation claims means retraining many shadow models. LiRA uses 256 (64 for ImageNet), and standard DP audits need hundreds to thousands of runs. On the framer's typical 288 GPU-hour paper, a LiRA audit is about 74,000 GPU-hours [estimate]. One-run audits are cheaper but give looser bounds.

R1:physical.title: Checking machine-unlearning claims
R1:physical.summary: The reference for unlearning is retraining without the data. One evaluation study used 10,240 models and calls strong per-example attacks on LLMs 'extremely computationally expensive'. The cheaper population attacks overestimate how much privacy unlearning gives. SISA's speed-up over retraining is only 1.36x on ImageNet.

R1:physical.title: Training-data attribution and data valuation
R1:physical.summary: These are counterfactual claims, so the exact check is retraining on many data subsets. Datamodels released predictions from 4 million trained networks. Earlier methods needed thousands of models; TRAK approximates them with a handful.

R1:physical.title: Architecture and hyperparameter search claims
R1:physical.summary: NAS-Bench-101 took over 100 TPU-years to train 5 million models. That one-off table replaced over 900 TPU-years of benchmarking. Template for review: precompute shared baseline and variant tables, so many T3 'under-tuned baseline' checks become lookups.

R1:physical.title: Scaling-law claims
R1:physical.summary: Chinchilla's reported confidence intervals would need over 600,000 runs, while the authors likely ran fewer than 500. Replicators could not retrain, so they re-fitted data extracted from the paper's plots and still found the error. When compute binds, re-analysing published data (T0b) is the fallback.

R1:physical.title: Open retraining of landmark science models
R1:physical.summary: AlphaFold2 shipped without training code. OpenFold retrained it in about 50,000 A100 GPU-hours, roughly 170x the framer's typical paper [estimate]. It reached about 90% of final accuracy in 1,500 GPU-hours (about 3%), so early-convergence runs can screen which claims deserve a full reproduction.

R1:physical.title: Broad benchmark evaluation of many models
R1:physical.summary: HELM covers 30 models x 42 scenarios x 7 metrics, and such benchmarks cost thousands of GPU-hours per model. Smart subsets cut compute 100x or more; tinyBenchmarks estimates MMLU from 100 examples. Spot-checking a paper's reported numbers is cheap; full re-evaluation is where compute binds.

R1:physical.title: Interpretability audits of large models
R1:physical.summary: Gemma Scope used over 20% of GPT-3's training compute and about 20 PiB of activations. OpenAI trained a 16M-latent SAE on GPT-4 over 40B tokens. Claims about a large model's internals are close to T4: outsiders can check them only through shared released artefacts.

R1:physical.title: Jailbreak and robustness evaluation of LLMs
R1:physical.summary: Best-of-N jailbreaking reached 89% (GPT-4o) and 78% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) success at 10,000 samples, with success following a power law in N. A robustness claim is only as strong as its attack budget. This also applies to prompt-injection defences for LLM reviewers.

R1:physical.title: Verifying that a claimed training run happened
R1:physical.summary: Forging a proof-of-learning costs at least as much as the training it claims. Governance proposals would have chip firmware save weight snapshots and keep training records for inspectors. Relevant to adversarial authors, but costly at scale.

R1:physical.title: Zero-knowledge proofs of ML inference
R1:physical.summary: zkLLM proves one full inference of a 13B-parameter model in under 15 minutes, with proofs under 200 kB. Cryptographic checking of model outputs is possible, but proof generation is compute-heavy compared with plain inference.

R1:physical.title: Formal verification of neural-network properties
R1:physical.summary: Verifying even simple properties of ReLU networks is NP-complete. Reluplex's showcase was ACAS Xu networks of 300 ReLU nodes. Certifying robustness claims in papers hits a hard complexity wall long before frontier scale.

R1:physical.title: Fuzzing at ecosystem scale (AISLE's home domain)
R1:physical.summary: OSS-Fuzz runs on 100,000 VMs and had helped fix over 10,000 vulnerabilities and 36,000 bugs by Aug 2023. Re-finding known bugs scales linearly, but each new bug needs exponentially more machines. Checking a reported flaw is cheap; brute-force search for new flaws has steep diminishing returns.

R1:physical.title: SAT-based computer-assisted proofs
R1:physical.summary: The Pythagorean triples proof took 2 days on 800 cores and is about 200 TB (68 GB compressed certificate). The Schur number five proof is 2 PB, checked with a formally verified checker. With an exact, mechanical oracle, compute is the whole cost; compact certificates make checking feasible.

R1:physical.title: Proof search for formal mathematics
R1:physical.summary: AlphaProof took up to three days per IMO 2024 problem and trained on millions of problems; its Lean proofs are checked mechanically. When claims can be formalised, compute goes into search and checking becomes trivial. This is the regime where repeated sampling scales well.

R1:physical.title: Checking cryptographic security claims
R1:physical.summary: RSA-240 took about 900 and RSA-250 about 2,700 core-years to factor. Security claims are tested by extrapolating from record computations, not by breaking deployed key sizes. This is the realistic model for frontier (T4) ML claims: check against smaller-scale runs and fitted trends.

R1:physical.title: Climate-model verification by ensemble
R1:physical.summary: Hardware and compiler changes break bit-for-bit reproducibility in climate models. CESM instead checks new runs against a 151-member, one-year ensemble, which is the most compute-intensive step and is rebuilt several times a year. Template for ML seed variance: build a reference seed ensemble once per benchmark or codebase, then check runs cheaply.

R1:physical.title: Reinterpreting LHC results
R1:physical.summary: RECAST preserves analyses in containers for exact re-execution, which is now mandatory for new ATLAS Run 2 searches, at the CPU cost of full processing. Most reinterpretation uses fast approximate simulation. Simulation took over half of LHC computing, with a projected 4x CPU shortfall by 2027. Mandated preservation removes the agent-capability barrier and leaves compute as the binding limit.

R1:interp.title: Entity-hallucination probes on the reviewer
R1:interp.summary: Linear probes flag fabricated names, dates and citations in a model's own output: AUC 0.90 vs 0.71 for semantic entropy on Llama-3.3-70B (arxiv.org/abs/2509.03531). Goodfire's RLFR uses such probes as RL rewards and test-time monitors and cut hallucinations in Gemma-3-12B-IT by 58% (goodfire.com/research/rlfr). Fit is moderate. It checks the reviewer's own claims, not the paper's references, which lookups already handle.

R1:interp.title: Grounding detectors per finding
R1:interp.summary: Lookback Lens is a linear classifier on how much each attention head looks at the source versus the model's own output. It detects unsupported content about as well as hidden-state or entailment detectors, and transfers from 7B to 13B (arxiv.org/abs/2407.07071). It would catch false flags that misread the paper, but not ones that quote correctly and reason badly. Untested on review.

R1:interp.title: Correctness and uncertainty probes as a triage filter
R1:interp.summary: Self-verification probes (arxiv.org/abs/2504.05419) and semantic entropy probes (arxiv.org/abs/2406.15927) read correctness or uncertainty from hidden states almost for free. To lift SPOT's 6.1% precision to 50% while keeping 80% of real flags, a filter would need about 80% recall at about 5% false positives [estimate]. Main risks: such detectors transfer poorly across datasets (arxiv.org/abs/2410.02707), and SPOT offers only 91 labelled errors.

R1:interp.title: Probe-first cascade architecture
R1:interp.summary: Goodfire's production pattern sends only probe-flagged items to an LLM judge. On Kimi K3 it reached about 93% recall at 5.5% false positives with 29-49x lower judge cost (goodfire.com/research/production-cyber-monitors-on-kimi-k3). At Rakuten, probes raised F1 from 51% to 96% over using the same model as a black-box judge (goodfire.com/research/rakuten-sae-probes-for-pii-detection). It fits AISLE-style triage, but the cost saving matters little when text review already costs under $1 per paper.

R1:interp.title: Prompt-injection and task-drift detectors at ingestion
R1:interp.summary: TaskTracker probes on activation deltas reach near-perfect ROC AUC out of distribution (arxiv.org/abs/2406.00799). Attention Tracker needs no training and spots the distracted attention heads (arxiv.org/abs/2411.00348). Goodfire and Baseten sell prompt-injection monitors for open models. These would form a good second layer after stripping hidden text, against papers that address AI reviewers. Untested on paper-length inputs or adaptive attacks.

R1:interp.title: Reward-hacking and shortcut monitors on experiment agents
R1:interp.summary: Goodfire's difference-of-means probes detect reward hacking in Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8 Max. They roughly match chain-of-thought monitors (+3.1% and -7.9% at matched false-positive rate) and predict hacks before the action (arxiv.org/abs/2609.19101). A cascade cut monitoring cost by 90%. This is the best Goodfire-specific fit for auditing agent-run experiments, but it does not raise agent capability (PaperBench execution 4.5%).

R1:interp.title: Performative-reasoning probes
R1:interp.summary: Goodfire's Reasoning Theater shows attention probes decode the final answer early while the chain of thought still looks like deliberation. Early exit saved 68% of tokens on MMLU for DeepSeek-R1, with similar results on GPT-OSS-120B (goodfire.com/research/reasoning-theater). It could flag reviewers whose verdict is fixed before the analysis. Evidence is from multiple-choice tasks only. Fit is weak to moderate.

R1:interp.title: Auditing and steering reviewer biases
R1:interp.summary: Candidate tools are persona vectors for sycophancy (arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509), SHIFT feature ablation (arxiv.org/abs/2403.19647) and auditing games (arxiv.org/abs/2503.10965). Fit is weak. Prompting beats steering (arxiv.org/abs/2501.17148), removing author names fixes prestige bias more simply, and no study applies these tools to LLM reviewers.

R1:interp.title: Truth-direction probes on the paper's own statements
R1:interp.summary: Simple true or false statements are linearly represented and can be edited causally (arxiv.org/abs/2310.06824). However, probes generalise poorly (arxiv.org/abs/2307.00175), and the evidence covers short facts, not empirical ML claims. Speculative. Cannot replace T3 experiments.

R1:interp.title: Membership and memorisation checks on released checkpoints
R1:interp.summary: This is the only option that touches T3 compute. A membership test could flag test-set contamination without retraining. The demonstrated method, Min-K% Prob, is black-box (arxiv.org/abs/2310.16789). Goodfire's loss-curvature and predictive data-debugging methods target the developer's own training, not third-party audits, and are self-described as immature. Speculative.

R1:interp.title: Representational similarity for routing the swarm
R1:interp.summary: Model errors are correlated (arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962), and SAE feature spaces are highly similar across LLMs (arxiv.org/abs/2410.06981), so one could pick swarm members whose representations differ. No evidence shows that representational difference predicts independent errors. Routing by error category, as SPOT's results suggest, is cheaper and evidenced. Speculative.

R1:interp.title: Circuit-level audits of individual reviewer decisions
R1:interp.summary: Attribution graphs are limited to prompts of about 100 tokens, take over an hour each to analyse, and may miss key computation (transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html). Not viable per paper. Possibly useful offline to diagnose recurring reviewer failure classes on short excerpts.

R2:physical.title: Board games (Go, chess, Hex)
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound. The rules are the simulator, so there is no sim-to-real gap. AlphaZero got superhuman from rules alone using 5,000 TPUs for self-play (arxiv.org/abs/1712.01815). In Hex, strength rises about 500 Elo per 10x compute, perfect play needs 7x more compute per board-size step, and 10x train-time compute replaces about 15x test-time compute (arxiv.org/abs/2104.03113).

R2:physical.title: Large simulated video games (Dota 2, StarCraft II)
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound. OpenAI Five used 770±50 PFlops/s-days over 10 months to beat the world champions. Its authors name compute scale as key for any game that can run in parallel across hundreds of thousands of copies, though they note data quality matters even more (arxiv.org/abs/1912.06680). Each AlphaStar agent got about 200 years of play on 16 TPUs over 14 days (deepmind.google). The Rubik's-cube hand spent a similar budget on one rigid object (arxiv.org/pdf/1910.07113).

R2:physical.title: Turbulent flow by direct numerical simulation
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound. The Navier-Stokes equations are solved with no turbulence model, and cost grows as Re^3. Most industrial flows are beyond the largest computers (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_numerical_simulation). My arithmetic: 1000x more compute buys only about 10x in Reynolds number. The cheap workarounds (RANS, LES) give up accuracy to save compute.

R2:physical.title: Weather and climate at kilometre scale
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound on resolution. Going from 50 km to 2 km grids costs at least about 15,000x more, and 4,888 GPUs gave only 0.043 simulated years per day at 930 m. Long climate runs would need about 100x more speed (gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/1665/2018/). The ML route (GraphCast) works because four decades of ERA5 reanalysis data already exist (deepmind.google). Robotics has no equivalent dataset.

R2:physical.title: Molecular dynamics and protein folding
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound on timescale, model-bound on force fields. Time steps are about 1 fs, and runs past about 1 µs are prohibitively expensive (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_dynamics). Anton 3 is custom silicon that simulates a million atoms at over 100 µs per day (scholars.duke.edu/publication/1503431). Force-field bias, such as AMBER ff03 over-stabilizing helices, persists however long the run (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4487363).

R2:physical.title: Electronic structure and materials discovery (DFT)
R2:physical.summary: Mixed. DFT is accurate but expensive, and its exact exchange-correlation functional is unknown (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density_functional_theory). GNoME's loop of model proposals checked by DFT found 2.2M crystals, 380k of them highly stable, and outside labs made 736 of them (deepmind.google). Compute buys how many candidates get checked. The functional sets the accuracy ceiling.

R2:physical.title: Lattice QCD
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound, counting memory bandwidth as part of compute. It needs the largest supercomputers. Cost rises as the lattice spacing shrinks, results are extrapolated to zero spacing, and the bottleneck is memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lattice_QCD). The theory is exact, so discretization error is what compute buys down.

R2:physical.title: Physically based rendering for synthetic perception data (glassware)
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound for forming the image. Path tracing is Monte Carlo and often needs thousands of samples per pixel (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Path_tracing). Its error falls as 1/sqrt(N) (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_integration). ClearGrasp trained on 50k+ synthetic images of transparent objects and generalized to real ones (arxiv.org/abs/1910.02550). This is one part of dishwasher perception where compute buys accuracy, though the scene and material content still has to come from the real world.

R2:physical.title: High-fidelity contact and cloth simulation
R2:physical.summary: Partly compute-constrained, and the most relevant item for the framer's verdict. IPC gives contact guaranteed free of interpenetration at large scale (ipc-sim.github.io). Yarn-level cloth is accurate but slow: contact is the bottleneck and a garment takes hours (cs.cornell.edu/projects/YarnCloth; news.cornell.edu/node/269321). Compute could pay for this accuracy inside training loops, but fabric parameters must still be measured (arxiv.org/html/2310.09543, via framer).

R2:physical.title: Rigid in-hand dexterity with domain randomization
R2:physical.summary: Partly compute-bound. In OpenAI's Rubik's-cube work, wider automatic randomization tracked better sim-to-real transfer, and the longest, largest runs transferred best. But the team improved simulator fidelity during the same runs, so not all of the gain was compute (arxiv.org/pdf/1910.07113). DeXtreme and DextrAH-G were trained in GPU simulation (arxiv.org/abs/2210.13702; arxiv.org/abs/2407.02274). Locomotion already trains in minutes on one GPU (arxiv.org/abs/2109.11978).

R2:physical.title: Task-and-motion planning and dishwasher rack packing
R2:physical.summary: Compute-constrained when deciding what to do. Exact high-dimensional motion planning is intractable. Sampling-based planners succeed with probability approaching 1 as they get more time (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_planning). TAMP mixes discrete and continuous search (arxiv.org/abs/2010.01083), and bin packing is strongly NP-complete (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bin_packing_problem). Dish placement is a sub-problem that compute can buy. I found no source showing it is the binding limit in practice.

R2:physical.title: On-robot real-time policy inference
R2:physical.summary: Compute-constrained at deployment, through latency, power and cost. Figure's Helix runs a 7B model at 7-9 Hz and a 200 Hz controller on embedded low-power GPUs (figure.ai/news/helix). Gemini Robotics On-Device trails its cloud flagship slightly (deepmind.google). Physical Intelligence reports VLA latency of 100 ms or more, which its real-time chunking method addresses (pi.website/research/real_time_chunking). The responses so far are mostly architectural.

R2:physical.title: Training robot foundation models and video world models
R2:physical.summary: Compute-heavy and partly compute-bound. Cosmos used 10,000 H100s for three months on about 20M hours of video (arxiv.org/html/2501.03575v1). By my arithmetic that is about 21.6M GPU-hours. GEN-0 needs about 7B parameters to absorb its data (generalistai.com/blog/gen-0, via framer). These models inherit their data's gaps, including missing touch (rodneybrooks.com, via framer).

R2:interp.title: Latent-space generalization diagnostics (general vs memorized SAE features)
R2:interp.summary: SAEs trained on VLA activations separate reusable motion and semantic features from episode-specific memorization. The share of general features is largest in pi0.5-DROID and smallest in OpenVLA fine-tuned on LIBERO-Goal, so more diverse data appears to yield more reusable features. The authors propose this as a rollout-free proxy for generalization but have not tested it as one (arXiv 2603.19183). Goodfire's Silico makes the same pitch for robotics. It targets the framer's data-diversity and evaluation bottlenecks. Evidence: simulation plus DROID hardware. Rating: medium.

R2:interp.title: Causal tracing of why policies break (activation injection and patching)
R2:interp.summary: Activation injection in pi0.5 shows the learned motor program is bound to absolute workspace coordinates and ignores the scene: 99.6% of 1,968 episodes, and 50/50 empty-air grasps on a UR10e (arXiv 2603.19233). Goodfire's unnamed robotics case study found an information bottleneck midway through a model and unused past frames, but gives no numbers. This tells teams whether a failure needs more diverse data or a model change. It targets generalization to new homes. Rating: medium.

R2:interp.title: Runtime failure and state monitors built on internal features
R2:interp.summary: SAFE shows VLA internal features encode task success and failure across tasks. It was tested on OpenVLA, pi0 and pi0-FAST, in simulation and on real robots, and its alert lets the robot stop, back off or ask for help. FAIL-Detect and OpenVLA symbolic-state probes (>0.90 accuracy) are related work. Goodfire's production probes (Rakuten F1 51% to 96%, 10-500x cheaper, better synthetic-to-real transfer) show the approach is cheap and deployable. Monitors do not raise per-item success; they turn damage into interventions. Rated the most deployment-ready option. Rating: high.

R2:interp.title: Data attribution, curation and choosing what to collect next
R2:interp.summary: CUPID estimates each demonstration's influence on success: under 33% of curated data gives state-of-the-art RoboMimic policies, with similar gains in hardware, and it isolates spurious correlations. DemInf filtering adds 5-10%. Goodfire's probe-based attribution cut a target behaviour by 63% at a tenth of the cost, and predictive data debugging forecasts learned behaviours before training (R^2 = 0.9), both LLM-only so far. This is the strongest lever on the framer's number-one data bottleneck, but it cannot create the missing touch modality. Rating: high.

R2:interp.title: Inference-time activation steering of physical behaviour
R2:interp.summary: Haon et al. found sparse speed and direction directions and steered pi0 and OpenVLA with no fine-tuning, in LIBERO and on a UR5. SAE features also steer on DROID hardware, but many clean features have unpredictable effects, and aggressive interventions expose safety limits. Goodfire's mountain-car work shows linear steering can produce garbled states, so steering should follow the curved manifold. A gentle-grip knob for stemware is an obvious use, but no paper has shown one. Rating: low-medium.

R2:interp.title: Mechanistic (head-targeted) fine-tuning
R2:interp.summary: Robotic Steering uses few-shot demonstrations to find and fine-tune only task-specific attention heads. On a Franka arm it beat LoRA, with better robustness to task variation and lower compute (arXiv 2511.22697). It is a data-efficiency lever for adapting to a new home. The abstract gives no effect sizes. Rating: medium.

R2:interp.title: Probes as rewards or value signals for real-world RL
R2:interp.summary: Goodfire's RLFR used activation probes on a frozen model copy as RL rewards: 58% fewer hallucinations at about 90x lower cost than an LLM judge. pi*0.6 Recap's corrections are limited by a human's ability to spot when to intervene, and SAFE shows failure is decodable from VLA features. The proposal (an extrapolation) is that failure probes on a frozen policy could flag corrections or shape rewards. No robotics demonstration was found. Rating: speculative.

R2:interp.title: Rare-failure discovery and estimation with fewer trials
R2:interp.summary: Goodfire's model diff amplification made rare bad behaviours 10-300x more common, from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 30. It is for detecting behaviours, not measuring how often they occur. Logit Path Extrapolation matches naive sampling's AUROC with up to 30x fewer rollouts but needs a model in which the behaviour is common. Both target the framer's 99.9% evaluation problem, but both rely on LLM logits and are untested on action policies. Rating: speculative.

R2:interp.title: Representation-level sim-to-real diagnostics
R2:interp.summary: OpenAI's Rubik's-cube policy stored inferred physics parameters in its LSTM state: cube size decoded at over 80%, mass at 50-60%, with the stored information tracking randomization (ADR) entropy. Co-training analysis shows transfer depends on balancing cross-domain alignment against domain discernibility. Encoder invariance and action scores predict Sim2Real transfer. These tools show whether a policy uses its randomization and whether its vision will transfer. They cannot fix the cloth simulator's model-form error. Rating: low-medium.

R2:interp.title: Extracting physics from learned models to fix simulators (Goodfire discovery pattern)
R2:interp.summary: Symbolic regression on GNN internals recovers force laws that generalize out of distribution better than the network itself. MeshGraphNets learn cloth simulation 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than the simulator they were trained on. Goodfire distilled SAE features of an Alzheimer's model into a simple fragment-length classifier (small cohort, wide confidence intervals). The extrapolation: learn real cloth and wet-friction dynamics, then interpret them into better simulator models. It is the only route that attacks model-form error directly. Unproven for cloth, and it still needs real measurements. Rating: speculative, highest ceiling.

R2:interp.title: Auditing world and video models for physical structure before trusting their data
R2:interp.summary: Video generators generalize case-by-case and fail out of distribution, and scaling alone is insufficient (Kang et al.). On Physics-IQ, physical understanding is unrelated to visual realism. Representation-space predictors show intuitive physics where pixel-space models perform near chance. Goodfire's mountain-car world model shows physical variables living on curved manifolds, and Silico pitches latent-space physics checks before any frame is generated. This is a cheap filter on DreamGen-style synthetic data. Rating: low-medium.

R2:interp.title: Capacity, interference and memorization analysis for long-tail skills
R2:interp.summary: Huang et al. (listed by Goodfire) show smaller models spend neurons on frequent tasks and lose rare, complex ones through gradient interference; larger OLMo models retain them. GEN-0 reports ossification at 1B parameters and a phase transition at 7B. Goodfire's loss-curvature method separates memorization from generalization in the weights. Together these give a mechanistic reason long-tail items like wine glasses are dropped by small policies, and a guide for model sizing and data mixtures. Untested on robot policies. Rating: low-medium.

R3:physical.title: Regional physics-based ground-motion simulation (EQSIM / SW4)
R3:physical.summary: COMPUTE-BOUND. Compute is named as the barrier: regional simulations were held to about 0-2 Hz, while engineering needs about 0-10 Hz. Cost rises 16x per doubling of frequency, so 2 to 10 Hz is 625x harder. Frontier now runs Hayward and San Andreas scenarios at 8-10 Hz on grids of about 500 billion points. The next limit is fine-scale geology data.

R3:physical.title: Simulation-based seismic hazard (CyberShake, RSQSim, UCERF3)
R3:physical.summary: COMPUTE-BOUND. CyberShake Study 22.12 used about 772k node-hours, mostly on Summit, for 335 sites and 420M seismograms, with the deterministic part at only 0-1 Hz. Fully dynamic sources are still 'computationally intractable' for PSHA. UCERF3's 1,440 logic-tree branches needed supercomputers. It works because long-term probability does not need today's fault stress.

R3:physical.title: Earthquake-cycle (SEAS) and dynamic-rupture simulation
R3:physical.summary: COMPUTE-BOUND as a simulation, NOT as a prediction. 3D benchmarks find recurrence and nucleation sensitive to grid resolution and domain size. The cheaper quasi-dynamic shortcut changes the results. The Kaikoura rupture took about 2 h on 3000 cores per run, so parameter sweeps are costly. Used to forecast a real fault, it still depends on unobserved stress and friction (C2).

R3:physical.title: Full-waveform seismic tomography (global adjoint and exploration FWI)
R3:physical.summary: Mostly compute-bound. Global models ran on Titan (18,688 GPUs) and Summit with a shortest period of 17 s. The authors expected Summit to reach 9 s and exascale a few seconds. 3D elastic FWI still needs efficiency gains. Starting models, missing low frequencies and station/event coverage are a second limit.

R3:physical.title: Geodynamo simulation
R3:physical.summary: Strongly compute-bound and far from its target. The best runs reach Ekman number 1e-7 'at the limit of what is feasible on today's supercomputers', against about 1e-15 for Earth's core. Cost grows 30-100x per decade of Ekman number, implying roughly 1e11-1e16x more compute (inference). Large-eddy simulation that reaches 1e-8 is the algorithmic workaround.

R3:physical.title: Global mantle convection and plate tectonics
R3:physical.summary: Mostly compute-bound in resolution. Adaptive mesh refinement on large parallel supercomputers brought global models to about 1 km scale and revealed subduction mechanics and plate speeds. Unknown rheology is the analogue of unknown fault friction.

R3:physical.title: Kilometre-scale weather and climate
R3:physical.summary: COMPUTE-BOUND. km-scale grids let convection be simulated rather than parameterized. ICON at 1 km is about 1500x short of 1 simulated year per day, and even a pre-exascale-sized machine reaches only about 0.06 SYPD. I/O and storage are an emerging limit. ML (GenCast: a 15-day ensemble in 8 min) changes the cost curve, because the atmosphere's state is observed.

R3:physical.title: Real-time tsunami inundation forecasting
R3:physical.summary: Compute-bound at real-time latency, and being relieved. The physics route needs a vector supercomputer for 10 m-grid inundation in under 20 min. An ML surrogate trained on 3,093 simulated scenarios with 150 offshore stations matches it at about 99% lower cost. The remaining limit is offshore sensor density.

R3:physical.title: Archive-scale earthquake detection and dense-array (DAS) processing
R3:physical.summary: Compute- and I/O-bound. Autocorrelation scales quadratically: about 20 years for 6 months of data, against about 2.4 days with FAST. LSH optimizations gave more than 100x speedup. 200 GPUs over weeks grew the SoCal catalogue to 1.81M events. DAS data volume (about 90 TB in PubDAS) limits distribution. This is the clearest payoff for GPUs near the earthquake problem.

R3:physical.title: Bayesian finite-fault source inversion and uncertainty quantification
R3:physical.summary: Compute-bound for the uncertainty quantification. Full Bayesian sampling was 'computationally intractable' at typical parameter counts until parallel samplers such as CATMIP. The width of the posterior is still set by surface-only data, which compute cannot narrow.

R3:physical.title: Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case)
R3:physical.summary: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND on the real Earth. A synthetic 2-D perfect-model test with 150 members forecast 70% of 21 events with the alarm on 17% of the time, against 68% for a periodic model. The runs were nearly embarrassingly parallel and about 20 members sufficed. On real faults, model error and unobserved deep stress (C2) bind first.

R3:interp.title: Audit forecasters and precursors for shortcuts and artifacts
R3:interp.summary: Use attribution, probes or SAE features to check whether a forecaster or precursor claim rests on physics or on artifacts: station noise, GPS common-mode noise, catalogue completeness, train/test leakage. Seismology has precedents. A 2-parameter regression matched the 13,451-parameter DeVries aftershock network (Mignan & Broccardo, arxiv.org/abs/1904.01983), and lab-quake Kaggle teams practised data snooping (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7865129/). Ready now and cheap. It cuts false positives but does not touch C1-C3.

R3:interp.title: Trace forecast skill back to the training events
R3:interp.summary: Probe-based data attribution in the style of Goodfire (goodfire.com/research/probe-based-data-attribution) ranks the training events that drive a forecaster's skill, then confirms by editing the data and retraining. Inference: it would show whether skill on large events rests on a few sequences. That is the same issue as the dispute over Bletery & Nocquet's stacked GPS signal, where critics say dropping a few noisy events removes it. It measures C3. Ready now.

R3:interp.title: Distil the model into a compact law
R3:interp.summary: Once interp has found what drives a model, refit a few-parameter or symbolic model on those variables. Precedents: Cranmer et al. symbolic regression (arxiv.org/abs/2006.11287), Goodfire's 11-feature Alzheimer's regression, and the lab friction equation of state (doi.org/10.1002/2017GL076708). Inference: few parameters are cheaper to validate prospectively in CSEP, which eases C3. A distilled law cannot exceed the skill of the model it came from.

R3:interp.title: Carry interpreted lab features to real faults
R3:interp.summary: Find the stress-encoding signal features in models trained on lab faults, where stress is measured, then search field data for them. Precedents: the hidden lab acoustic signal (doi.org/10.1002/2017GL074677), the friction fingerprint, signal energy tracking the slow-slip cycle in Cascadia, and PINNs improving transfer (doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-39377-6). It works around C3, but C2 and the open question of generalizing from lab to Earth remain.

R3:interp.title: Use simulators to test whether models learned the physics
R3:interp.summary: Apply Vafa et al.'s inductive-bias probe (arxiv.org/abs/2507.06952) with earthquake-cycle simulators (RSQSim, community benchmark problems) where stress is known. The test is whether waveform foundation models learn rate-and-state dynamics or task-specific heuristics. It diagnoses C1 and C4. It is limited by the gap between simulation and reality, and I found no seismology application.

R3:interp.title: Probe models for a latent fault state (Othello-style)
R3:interp.summary: Train linear or nonlinear probes on seismic foundation models such as SeisLM for stress, friction or time to failure, on lab and simulator data first and then on field data. Precedents: Othello-GPT's board state (arxiv.org/abs/2210.13382, 2309.00941), AlphaZero chess concepts, and Goodfire's Evo 2 phylogeny manifold. Inference: unlike the Othello board, crustal stress does not follow from the inputs, so the probes directly test where C2 loses the information.

R3:interp.title: Mine waveform models for new signal classes (the Evo 2 template)
R3:interp.summary: Run SAEs or manifold discovery on pretrained waveform or GPS models to catalogue the signal classes they have learned (tremor, repeating quakes, slow slip, artifacts), as Goodfire did with Evo 2 (goodfire.com/blog/interpreting-evo-2). The payoff is mostly monitoring. Candidate precursors found this way face the same single-event noise-floor problem as the GPS signal. Known SAE limits apply, including results matched by simpler baselines and curved structure being fragmented.

R4:physical.title: Numerical verification of a conjecture up to a bound
R4:physical.summary: Riemann-zero checks to 3e12 used about 7.5M core-hours (arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09765). Goldbach was checked to 4e18 using 781.8 CPU-years, and the double-check stopped at 4e17 (sweet.ua.pt/tos/goldbach.html). The statement is one line, the work parallelizes trivially, and the bound reached grows with core-hours. It never proves the conjecture itself.

R4:physical.title: Exact enumeration and counting
R4:physical.summary: The 9th Dedekind number took 5,311 A100 GPU-hours (arxiv.org/pdf/2304.00895) and, independently, 47,000 FPGA-hours, about 3 months (arxiv.org/pdf/2304.03039). The binding limits are physical: hardware time, plus bit-flip risk (about 0.235 expected errors) that was handled by recomputing every result, not by expert review.

R4:physical.title: SAT resolution of finite combinatorial statements
R4:physical.summary: Pythagorean triples took about 35k CPU-hours and produced a 200 TB proof. Schur number 5 took over 14 CPU-years and produced a 2 PB proof. Keller dimension 7 and the empty hexagon (about 17.3k CPU-hours, near-linear speedup on 1,000 instances) are similar. Better encodings cut the bill 10-500x. The only trust gap, the encoding, was closed once by a Lean formalization (arXiv 2403.17370).

R4:physical.title: Exhaustive case analysis with formal certificates
R4:physical.summary: BB(5) was proved in Coq over 181M machines (arXiv 2509.12337). R(4,5)=25 was checked in HOL4 in under 950 CPU-days, and memory was the main limit (arXiv 2404.01761). R(5,5)<=46 took about 30 CPU-years plus a 50 CPU-year independent replication (arXiv 2409.15709). The family turns math-bound at BB(6): the Collatz-like 'Antihydra' machine cannot be decided by simulation (wiki.bbchallenge.org/wiki/Antihydra).

R4:physical.title: Checking huge certificates
R4:physical.summary: Checking costs about as much as producing the proof: 16k CPU-hours for Pythagorean triples, about 36 CPU-years for Schur 5, and about 5,000 Azure processor-hours for Flyspeck's 23k inequalities in HOL Light (arxiv.org/pdf/1501.02155). The same pressure shows up in Lean CI and RAM costs. These are real budget lines that grow with proof size, but they are not the binding constraint.

R4:physical.title: Proof search on fixed, already-vetted formal statements
R4:physical.summary: Seed-Prover 1.5 reports a log-linear solve rate against compute, at 10-40 H20-days per problem. It quotes AlphaProof at about 500 TPU-days per problem (arxiv.org/html/2512.17260). At IMO 2024 AlphaProof took up to 3 days per problem on human-formalized statements. This is compute-bound only when the statement is already trusted; on fresh statements, search mostly turns up misformalizations.

R4:physical.title: Training provers by RL against the Lean kernel
R4:physical.summary: AlphaProof trained on millions of autoformalized problems over weeks. Goedel-Prover-V2 used Lean compiler feedback for RL and ran data generation on 144 H100s. This is more compute-bound than proof search (F) because a misformalized training statement is still a valid Lean problem, so fidelity does not limit training. The binding inputs are GPU time and problems of the right difficulty.

R4:physical.title: Construction search scored by an automatic evaluator
R4:physical.summary: FunSearch produced the largest cap-set improvement in 20 years. AlphaEvolve found 48-multiplication 4x4 complex matrix multiplication and an 11-dimensional kissing number of 593, and improved about 20% of 50+ problems. Cost scales with LLM calls, and setup takes hours. A 'cheating phenomenon' (leaky verifiers, exploited numerical integration; arxiv.org/html/2511.02864) is the fidelity layer, but it is paid once per evaluator, not once per paper.

R4:physical.title: Computer-assisted proofs in analysis and mathematical physics
R4:physical.summary: Flyspeck needed about 5,000 processor-hours. Chen-Hou's 3D Euler blowup proof relies on rigorous computer-assisted numerics (arXiv 2305.05660). DeepMind's unstable singularities reached near float64 precision, limited by GPU round-off, which is enough to begin computer-assisted proofs (arXiv 2509.14185). The binding limits are processor-hours and arithmetic precision, but only after human analysis has reduced the problem to finite checks.

R4:interp.title: Activation monitors for agent cheating
R4:interp.summary: Difference-of-means probes on the agent's activations that flag reward hacking. In Goodfire's work they catch hacks about as well as CoT monitors, fire before the hacking action, and cut LLM-monitoring cost by about 90% in a cascade. In Lean they would target dummy definitions, weakened lemmas and sorry offloading earlier than CI, beyond what Comparator's static checks catch. Untested on Lean, and vulnerable to obfuscation if a model is trained against them. Good fit.

R4:interp.title: Hallucination probes for invented lemmas and citations
R4:interp.summary: Entity-level linear probes (AUC 0.90 vs 0.71 for semantic entropy; also detect wrong math answers) aimed at the AlphaProof Nexus failure, where an invented 'established result' is left as a sorry. Hallucinated Mathlib lemma names already fail to compile, so the value is in natural-language blueprints. Untested on mathematical citations.

R4:interp.title: Latent-knowledge probes for statement fidelity
R4:interp.summary: Probes on a formalizer or auditor that predict 'misformalized' when the model internally knows its Lean differs from the English (ELK-style; Mallen et al. recover 89% of the AUROC gap). This is the only option aimed at the core bottleneck. It fails when every model shares the misreading, and LLM errors are correlated. It can be trained on the Formal Conjectures and PutnamBench fix pairs. Untested; §7 proposes the experiment.

R4:interp.title: Cross-representation comparison of English and Lean
R4:interp.summary: Compare middle-layer representations of the informal and formal statements, building on the semantic hub result that code and arithmetic share a space with language. It would be a meaning-level check that does not depend on what the auditor writes, but nothing shows it can separate fine distinctions such as natural vs lower density, and SAE features capture concepts only in fragments. Most speculative option.

R4:interp.title: Fork mapping of translation choices
R4:interp.summary: Resample the formalizer to find the tokens where the formal meaning forks (for example Fin 3 → ℝ vs EuclideanSpace), using Forking Paths, Goodfire's Forking Fast or Thought Anchors, so experts review only the forks. It finds model uncertainty, not author ambiguity, and a confident shared misreading produces no fork. Mostly a black-box method.

R4:interp.title: Probes as cheap verifiers and search guides
R4:interp.summary: Correctness probes for early exit (24% fewer tokens) and probe-guided accept/reject of search steps (Goodfire self-correcting search, Pareto optimal) to prune dead-end decompositions. Lowers proof-search cost, which framer.md already finds cheap. Does not touch fidelity.

R4:interp.title: Features as rewards (RLFR) for training formalizers
R4:interp.summary: Use probe scores as RL rewards, as Goodfire's RLFR did: 58% fewer hallucinations, about 90x cheaper per intervention than an LLM judge, with probes run on a frozen copy of the model. It could train formalizers not to cheat or hallucinate. Optimising against a monitor risks obfuscation (Baker et al., Bailey et al.), so a probe used for training cannot also be the final audit.

R4:interp.title: Probe-based data attribution
R4:interp.summary: Rank fine-tuning data by the activation-difference signal it carries. Goodfire cut an unwanted behaviour by 63–78% for about $30 of compute. It could find the data that teaches provers to cheat or to adopt default readings. Mathlib's conventions are not errors in themselves, so this helps build cleaner provers but is marginal for fidelity.

R4:interp.title: Model-diff amplification and rare-failure estimation
R4:interp.summary: Amplify the logit difference between a model before and after post-training (rare behaviours become 10–300x more common), or use Logit Path Extrapolation (30x fewer rollouts), to surface cheating propensities that RL instils in a prover before deployment. These detect such behaviours but do not measure the residual misformalization rate, which still needs a human gold set.

R4:interp.title: Circuit-level audit of disputed cases
R4:interp.summary: Use attribution graphs or SAE features to explain why a formalizer chose a reading. In Anthropic's auditing game, 3 of 4 teams found a hidden objective this way, but attribution graphs give satisfying insight on only about a quarter of prompts. Useful for research, but as a per-statement tool it consumes the same scarce expert time it is meant to save.

R5:physical.title: Turbulent fluid flow (direct numerical simulation)
R5:physical.summary: Compute-bound in the framer's strict sense. The Navier-Stokes equations are trusted, and DNS cost grows as Re^3, so compute buys resolution that removes turbulence-closure error. Contact and cloth have no tractable trusted fine-scale equation to resolve in the same way.

R5:physical.title: Kilometer-scale weather and climate simulation
R5:physical.summary: Compute-bound. At kilometer resolution, convection is resolved instead of parameterized: SCREAM ran at 3.25 km on Frontier, and a full Earth-system run reached 1.25 km at 145.7 simulated days per day on 20,480 GH200s. Throughput is still the binding input.

R5:physical.title: Molecular dynamics of biomolecules
R5:physical.summary: Compute-bound on timescale: steps are about 1 fs, and runs beyond about 1 microsecond are prohibitively expensive, which justified the special-purpose Anton machines (about 17 us/day versus a few hundred ns/day on general-purpose codes). Bounded by the model class on chemistry, because force fields cannot break bonds.

R5:physical.title: DFT-driven materials discovery
R5:physical.summary: The labels are computed, so a data flywheel becomes a compute flywheel: GNoME found 2.2M stable structures with power-law data scaling, and OMat24 released 110M DFT calculations. The approximated exchange-correlation functional and real-world synthesis set a structural ceiling.

R5:physical.title: Learned weather emulators (GraphCast)
R5:physical.summary: Trained on four decades of ERA5 reanalysis, it beats operational systems on 90% of 1,380 targets and forecasts in under a minute on one TPU v4. It shows a learned simulator becoming compute-bound because a trusted corpus already existed. Robotics has no equivalent corpus for contact.

R5:physical.title: In-hand manipulation of rigid objects
R5:physical.summary: The robotics problem with the best evidence of being compute-bound. The Rubik's cube run used 64 V100s plus 920 32-core workers for months (about 13k simulated years), and scaling ADR up vastly improved sim2real transfer. It was still partly fidelity-bound, at 20-60% success, and Visual Dexterity dropped an unseen object in 56% of trials.

R5:physical.title: Legged and humanoid locomotion
R5:physical.summary: Compute-solved. Rough-terrain walking trains in 20 minutes on one GPU, and a humanoid transformer controller transferred zero-shot. PPO stops benefiting from more parallel environments beyond a certain point, so algorithms, not FLOPs, are now the limit.

R5:physical.title: Agile flight and drone racing (Swift)
R5:physical.summary: Compute-solved, with a robot-side residual. It trained in 50 minutes on one workstation and used about 50 s of real flight to fit perception and dynamics residuals. It beat champions in 15 of 25 races. Onboard it is runtime-bound: gate detection takes 40 ms on a Jetson TX2.

R5:physical.title: Tokamak plasma magnetic control
R5:physical.summary: Compute-friendly physical control with a trusted equilibrium model. It used 5,000 actors for 1-3 days and transferred zero-shot to TCV at 10 kHz. The simulator's known gaps (transport, poorly represented regions) are avoided rather than modelled, which a household robot cannot do.

R5:physical.title: Driving decision-making in object-level simulation (GIGAFLOW)
R5:physical.summary: Compute-bound inside the abstraction: 1.6B km of self-play with no human data, 4.4B transitions per hour on one 8-GPU node, and state-of-the-art results on CARLA, nuPlan and Waymax. Perception is abstracted away and the work stayed entirely in simulation.

R5:physical.title: Collision-free arm motion planning
R5:physical.summary: Geometry is exact, so planning is bound by compute at runtime and for data generation. cuRobo averages 50 ms (60x faster) with GPU-parallel seeds. Motion Policy Networks trained only in simulation on 3M problems in 500k environments and transferred to a real robot.

R5:physical.title: Grasp synthesis for rigid objects
R5:physical.summary: Dataset generation is compute-bound because analytic or force-closure labels are close to reality for rigid, quasi-static grasps. Dex-Net 2.0 used 6.7M synthetic samples and reached 93% on adversarial objects. DexGraspNet produced 1.32M grasps validated in Isaac Gym.

R5:physical.title: Outer-loop design search (robot morphology and reward code)
R5:physical.summary: Compute-bound by construction, since every candidate costs an inner RL run. DERL evaluated 4,000 morphologies on 1,152 CPUs in under 16 hours, and Eureka's evolutionary reward search beat human experts on 83% of 29 environments. Real-world value is capped by the fidelity of the scoring simulator.

R5:physical.title: Onboard inference for large robot policies (VLAs)
R5:physical.summary: Runtime-bound. π0 takes 73 ms per inference on an RTX 4090. Inference pauses between action chunks are absent from training data, which Physical Intelligence's real-time chunking addresses. Gemini Robotics On-Device trades some performance for local compute. This is the main way current laundry systems are compute-limited.

R5:physical.title: Real-time whole-body and contact-rich MPC
R5:physical.summary: Runtime-bound. iLQR runs at about 50 Hz with a 0.35-0.5 s horizon on a desktop CPU, and the humanoid's contacts were cut to two spheres per foot to fit the time budget. Real-time reasoning over contact modes is the stated historical obstacle, so more compute directly buys model detail here.

R5:physical.title: High-fidelity cloth and deformable contact simulation
R5:physical.summary: Throughput-bound. Cloth steps cost milliseconds at 100 Hz. IPC is robust but heavy, and GPU IPC slows as stiffness rises (StiffGIPC reports up to 10x speedup). Yarn-level knit simulation resolves microstructure but is slower and still approximates friction. Faster simulation does not mean correct simulation, which still needs measurement.

R5:physical.title: Rendering and tactile-sensor simulation
R5:physical.summary: Throughput-bound and being solved by engineering. ManiSkill3 renders 10-1000x faster (30,000+ FPS), TacSL simulates visuotactile sensors over 200x faster, and the Rubik's cube pipeline sized its rendering pool so rendering was not the bottleneck. This addresses perception throughput, not fidelity.

R5:physical.title: Video world models as learned robot simulators
R5:physical.summary: Constrained by both training and generation compute: Cosmos used 10,000 H100s for 3 months on about 20M hours of video, and GR00T neural trajectories take 2 GPU-minutes per second for a +5.8% real gain. Limited above all by the lack of a trusted contact-rich interaction corpus. It would become frontier-bound if such a corpus existed.

R5:interp.title: Data attribution and curation for real robot data
R5:interp.summary: Influence-function or probe-based attribution ranks real demonstrations by how they affect the policy and points to what to collect next. CUPID reached state-of-the-art diffusion policies on RoboMimic using under 33% of the data after curation (arxiv.org/abs/2506.19121). Goodfire's probe-based attribution runs at about one tenth the cost of a gradient method (goodfire.com/research/probe-based-data-attribution). This raises the information yield per fleet-hour, but the fleet is still needed.

R5:interp.title: Physics audits of learned world models before training policies in them
R5:interp.summary: Probe and intervene on world-model latents to test whether they encode physical variables or only memorized cases. Video models can look realistic without understanding physics (arxiv.org/abs/2501.09038) and generalize by nearest case rather than by law (arxiv.org/abs/2411.02385). Goodfire demonstrated latent steering on a toy mountain-car world model. Probing for cloth properties needs measured labels, which are scarce.

R5:interp.title: Symbolic distillation of learned simulators to fix the model class M
R5:interp.summary: Train a learned dynamics model on real cloth or contact data, then distill its learned interactions into symbolic equations to find the missing physics, such as rate dependence or hysteresis. Cranmer et al. recovered force laws this way, and the extracted equations generalized out of distribution better than the network (arxiv.org/abs/2006.11287). This is the most direct attack on the structural simulator gap, but it has not been shown on real cloth or friction.

R5:interp.title: Probing domain-randomized policies for implicit system identification
R5:interp.summary: Proposal. Probe a memory policy's hidden state to decode the randomized physics parameters in simulation, then read those probes during real rollouts. Stable, in-range estimates indicate a parametric gap that more compute can close. Drifting or saturated estimates indicate the real world is outside the simulator family, a structural gap compute cannot fix. Goodfire's finding that a customer's robot model ignored previous frames shows this kind of check matters.

R5:interp.title: Mechanistic diagnosis of VLA generalization failures
R5:interp.summary: Sparse autoencoders and activation injection show that pi0.5's motor programs are tied to absolute workspace coordinates. When the object was moved 10-15 cm, the arm grasped at the old coordinates in 50 of 50 real trials (arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233). Probes decode OpenVLA's object and action states with accuracy above 0.90. This separates failures that call for more diverse data from failures that call for architecture changes, without collecting data first. All evidence so far is on rigid pick-and-place.

R5:interp.title: Activation monitors and rare-failure estimation for reliability
R5:interp.summary: Probe-based runtime monitors, from OpenVLA state monitoring to Goodfire's reward-hacking probes (which cut LLM monitoring cost by 90%), could flag slip, failed knots, or a sim-trained policy exploiting simulator artifacts. Goodfire-listed logit extrapolation estimated rare LLM failure rates with up to 30x fewer rollouts, which suggests estimating rare robot failures with fewer real trials. The monitoring and extrapolation evidence is LLM-only.

R5:interp.title: Probes as reward signals and success detectors for deformables
R5:interp.summary: Goodfire's RLFR used probes on a frozen model as RL rewards, cutting hallucinations 58% at about 90x lower cost per intervention than an LLM judge. Self-correcting search used a probe to steer a materials generator. A probe on a frozen video model could score fold quality or knot security for real-world RL and autonomous data collection. Risks are the gap between simulated and real images and policies learning to fool the probe.

R5:interp.title: Activation steering of VLAs for adaptation without retraining
R5:interp.summary: Häon et al. steered pi0 and OpenVLA at inference time, changing height and speed on a real UR5, but only the low and slow directions worked (arxiv.org/abs/2509.00328). Robotic Steering fine-tunes only task-specific attention heads and reports beating LoRA. Steering between material-specific behavior modes could ease the cost of training one conservative policy for all materials, but it can only select behaviors the model already has.

R5:interp.title: Reading physical knowledge out of large real-data robot models
R5:interp.summary: Apply Goodfire's scientific-discovery pattern (Alzheimer's biomarkers from Pleiades, phylogeny geometry in Evo 2) to models like GEN-0 or pi0, trained on 10k to 270k+ hours of real data. The aim is to read out what they encode about fabric, friction, and knot security, then feed it into simulator terms, reward probes, or collection priorities. This needs access to proprietary weights, and what a policy learned may be too task-specific to transfer into a simulator.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?
